title: Ari's Wonderful Wobbly Trip
markdown:
Ari the rabbit loved to plan. Oh, how he loved to plan. Maps for his dandelion patch, schedules for his carrot-eating, even a clever colour-coded system for his sock drawer. Everything just so, like a tidy row of pebbles.

Every day he looked closely at those maps and schedules, dreaming of the perfect tea-on-the-train trip: neat cucumber sandwiches with the crusts cut off, perfectly brewed tea in pretty cups, polite chat, windows open to the sweet smell of flowers.

One day the sun peeked out with a particularly cheerful gleam, and Ari decided it was the perfect day. He invited his best friend, Wren the mole, always ready for excitement and tasty snacks, and his dear Aunt Dot, a wise old badger of the best advice and the warmest hugs. Wren's whiskers wiggled with joy. Aunt Dot smiled, eyes twinkling.

Ari packed practical bags for everyone. A neat little basket for Aunt Dot, woven with sturdy string. For Wren, a strong canvas bag, just right for treasures. For himself, a very organised travel case, many little sections, a satisfying click when it closed. He believed, with all his rabbit heart, that he had thought of everything, from a sudden shower to an unexpected sneeze. "Everything in its place," he'd mutter, patting each bag.

Bags can be a peculiar sort of thing. They have a way of taking on a personality, a little mischief tucked inside. Ari's carefully chosen bags were just waiting to show him that sometimes the best plans have a few happy wobbles.

The train journey began as you might expect. Ari sat by the window, a happy sigh, countryside rolling by. Wren sniffed for biscuits. Aunt Dot calmly knitted a wonderfully soft scarf, needles a soothing song. Then the bags started to stir. Not a loud noise. A playful rustle. A gentle shimmy.

First, Ari's travel case. It loved tidiness with all its might. As Ari reached for his perfectly folded napkin, the case gave a little whir and a click. Then, with a neat swoop, it rearranged all the sandwiches: cheese next to jam, cucumber next to egg. A way Ari found very confusing. "My dear boy," he whispered, brow furrowed, "what are you doing? The order is all wrong!"

Next, Wren's bag. An adventurer. It loved to explore. With a cheerful rustle it nudged Wren's elbow, zipper wiggling like a happy caterpillar. Out popped a shiny pebble Wren had found, then a smooth interesting twig, then — to Wren's surprise — a plump cheerful earthworm, who wiggled enthusiastically before being gently coaxed back inside. Wren giggled, tiny bells. "Hello there, Mr. Wriggles!"

Then Aunt Dot's basket, full of warmth like a hug. As she settled to knit, it gave a gentle creak and offered treasures: a warm woolly blanket that wrapped her; a small music box with a soft sleepy tune; a particularly delicious piece of fruitcake, plump raisins and candied peel, which she accepted with a happy sigh.

Ari, at first, felt a flutter of worry, a trapped butterfly in his tummy. His sensible plan was not sensible anymore. Sandwiches in the wrong order, the floor a miniature nature exhibit, Aunt Dot humming along to her basket. So unexpected.

He looked at Wren, sharing a crumb of fruitcake with his earthworm friend. He looked at Aunt Dot, calm and peaceful, needles dancing. He realised something that tickled his whiskers: the most sensible plan is sometimes the one that allows for a little happy surprise.

He took a deep breath, fruitcake and blooming flowers from the open window. The train rumbled, a gentle rocking. He decided to lean into the happy mess. He nudged his travel case. "Alright," a smile creeping, "perhaps the jam sandwiches do look rather nice next to the cheese. An interesting pattern."

The train pulled into a small charming station, late afternoon sun, perfect for tea. Ari set out the slightly jumbled sandwiches; to his surprise they looked quite cheerful. Wren offered his pebble collection; Aunt Dot admired each one. She shared fruitcake. The music box played. Cups clattered. Tea and baked goods. Warm golden friendship.

The tea wasn't served with perfectly folded napkins. It was served with a giggle, a wiggling earthworm, and a melody from a basket. It was the most wonderful tea Ari had ever had, far better than any he had planned.

Ever since, Ari still loved his plans, but he left a little room for wobbles. He wondered whether next time the travel case might alphabetise the jam — and whether Mr. Wriggles would require his own ticket, or merely a crumb and a kind word from Wren.
